claim: The agent.png image illustrates that agents are typically implemented as an LLM performing actions using tools, operating in continuous feedback loops, and used in situations where problems and solutions are unpredictable.

The image visually represents that agents have more autonomy than workflows and can make decisions about the tools they use and how to solve problems, while still allowing definition of the available toolset and guidelines for agent behavior.
To use TrackingState with a node-style hook to update agent state after a model call, define a custom AgentState subclass with the desired state fields, such as model_call_count.
Then, create an after_model node-style hook decorated with @after_model and specify the state_schema as TrackingState.
Inside the after_model hook function, accept the current state and runtime as parameters and return a dictionary with the updated state fields, for example incrementing model_call_count by 1.
The returned dictionary from the node-style hook is merged into the agent state using the graph's reducers, updating the agent state accordingly.
The different response_format options that use StructuredResponseT in LangChain are: ToolStrategy[StructuredResponseT], ProviderStrategy[StructuredResponseT], type[StructuredResponseT], and None.
ToolStrategy[StructuredResponseT] uses tool calling for structured output.
ProviderStrategy[StructuredResponseT] uses provider-native structured output.
type[StructuredResponseT] is a schema type that automatically selects the best strategy based on model capabilities.
None means structured output is not explicitly requested.
The store_based_model middleware selects which model to use for a request by reading the user's preferred model from the Store using the user_id from the request's runtime context.
If the user's preferred model is found in the Store and is present in the predefined MODEL_MAP, the middleware overrides the request's model with the preferred model from MODEL_MAP.
If no preferred model is found or it is not in MODEL_MAP, the middleware does not change the model and proceeds with the original request model.
To update model profiles using data from models.dev in LangChain, first update the source data at models.dev through a pull request to its GitHub repository if needed.
Next, update additional fields and overrides in the file langchain_<package>/data/profile_augmentations.toml through a pull request to the LangChain integration package if needed.

Then, use the langchain-model-profiles CLI tool to pull the latest data from models.dev, merge in the augmentations, and update the profile data by running the command: langchain-profiles refresh --provider <provider> --data-dir <data_dir>.

This command downloads the latest data for the specified provider from models.dev, merges augmentations from profile_augmentations.toml in the specified data directory, and writes merged profiles to _profiles.py in that directory.
An example command to refresh profiles for the 'anthropic' provider is: uv run --with langchain-model-profiles langchain-profiles refresh --provider anthropic --data-dir langchain_anthropic/data.
The value function in reasoning_fig7 is used to assess the quality of reasoning steps and to search over multiple reasoning trajectories.
This approach improves reliability by generating a set of answers and then using the value function to pick the best one, rather than generating a single answer from the model.
The summarization_prompt is a text prompt that instructs the model to summarize an article about an invention following a specific schema.
It describes the parameters that the summary should include, such as invented_year, summary, inventors, concepts, and description.
The prompt is used as the system message content in a chat completion request to guide the model's output to match the structured ArticleSummary format.
This structured summarization approach is useful for transforming text content into a structured object for display or database population.
You can build React UIs for real-time agent interactions using LangChain's frontend streaming capabilities with the @useStream hook.
LangChain supports streaming tokens directly from a chat model and streaming agent progress in real-time, which can be integrated into React UIs.
You can trace each step of a conversational loop, debug tool calls, and evaluate agent outputs with LangSmith.
To get set up for tracing, follow the tracing quickstart guide at /langsmith/trace-with-langchain.
It is recommended to also set up LangSmith Engine, which monitors your traces, detects issues, and proposes fixes.
Invoke an agent with a message and pass a thread_id so the agent can persist and resume conversation history, enabling tracing of the conversation state.
To enable LangSmith tracing, set environment variables LANGSMITH_TRACING=true and LANGSMITH_API_KEY with your API key.
Chat models accept context as a sequence of message objects, which include system instructions and human inputs, forming a growing list of messages over time.
Because context windows are limited, applications often use techniques to remove or "forget" stale information to manage the growing message list.
Interactions with chat models are often stateless, so each model invocation involves passing the entire accumulated list of messages as input.
Multi-turn agents accumulate long message histories, and tools like LangSmith can record each turn, tool result, and model response for inspection.
Model context includes the full list of messages (conversation history) sent to the model, along with system prompts, tools, model configuration, and response format.

Transient updates can modify messages sent to the model for a single call without changing saved state, while persistent updates modify the conversation history state using lifecycle hooks or commands.
LangChain standardizes model inputs and outputs to handle different provider-specific APIs and message formats, making it easy for developers to switch between models without lock-in.

For structured output, LangChain uses the `response_format` parameter to control how the agent returns structured data, supporting strategies like `ToolStrategy` for tool calling and `ProviderStrategy` for provider-native structured output.

When a schema type is provided directly for structured output, LangChain automatically selects `ProviderStrategy` if the model and provider support native structured output (e.g., OpenAI, Anthropic, xAI), otherwise it uses `ToolStrategy`.

LangChain normalizes provider-specific streaming formats (such as Anthropic's `thinking` blocks or OpenAI's `reasoning` summaries) into a standard `reasoning` content block type via the `content_blocks` property.
Provider-specific content blocks and escape hatches exist as `NonStandardContentBlock` with type `non_standard` to handle experimental or unique provider features.

You can customize a chat model's input size and capabilities by providing a custom model profile dictionary when initializing the chat model, specifying parameters such as 'max_input_tokens', 'tool_calling', and 'structured_output'.
A custom profile can be passed to the 'init_chat_model' function using the 'profile' parameter to overwrite or update model profile data.
Chat models accept parameters that configure behavior, including model name, provider, authentication key, randomness (temperature), and maximum tokens for output length.
You can create runtime-configurable models by specifying configurable fields such as 'model', 'model_provider', 'temperature', and 'max_tokens', allowing dynamic changes to model parameters.

Defining essential connections in a graph-based system allows nodes to handle their own routing logic, keeping control flow explicit and traceable so the next action is always understandable by looking at the current node.

Edges define how logic is routed and how the graph decides to stop, with types including normal edges for static routing and conditional edges for dynamic routing, affecting how nodes communicate and control flow proceeds.
A node can have multiple outgoing edges, and if so, all destination nodes execute in parallel in the next superstep, influencing control flow concurrency.
Choosing one routing mechanism per node—either normal edges or conditional edges/Command—is important to avoid mixed paths that complicate reasoning about graph behavior and control flow.
Conditional edges use routing functions that determine which node(s) to route to next after execution, enabling optional routing or termination and thus dynamic control flow.
Nodes declare possible next nodes using type hints with Command objects, making routing explicit and traceable, which structures control flow clearly within the graph.
Using Command objects in nodes allows combining state updates and routing decisions in a single function, enabling both control flow and state changes to be managed together.
Conditional entry points allow starting at different nodes based on custom logic, affecting initial control flow routing in the graph.

A system can keep track of conversation history without exceeding the model's input size limit by managing short-term memory with strategies such as trimming messages, deleting messages from state, summarizing messages, managing checkpoints, or using custom strategies like message filtering.

Summarization middleware can be used to automatically condense conversation history when it gets too long by summarizing older messages and replacing them with a summary that is permanently saved for future turns, while keeping recent messages intact.

Summarization middleware triggers based on thresholds such as token count or message count and controls how much context to preserve after summarization by specifying a fraction, token count, or number of recent messages to keep.
Trimming messages involves removing the first or last N messages before calling the LLM to keep the message history within the context window without deleting messages from state.

GPT enhances finding relevant information from large amounts of data by combining generative capabilities with retrieval components that access large corpora, enabling suggestions based on wide-ranging knowledge.
GPT can answer questions about unfamiliar topics by using a two-step Search-Ask method: first searching a library of text for relevant sections, then asking GPT with the retrieved text.
GPT can augment existing search systems by mimicking human browsing behavior and by retrieval with embeddings, which finds content most related to a query using cosine similarity.
Because GPT models have a limited maximum text length they can process at once, using a Search-Ask approach is recommended to draw upon large quantities of text.
Retrieval Augmented Generation (RAG) allows fetching relevant information from a database to generate answers, reducing hallucinations and providing up-to-date, relevant information.
The email agent uses a node called 'Classify Intent' which employs a large language model (LLM) to analyze the email content and classify its intent, urgency, topic, and summary.
The classification is done by invoking a structured LLM with a prompt containing the email content and sender email, which returns a structured dictionary with the classification results.

Based on the classification's 'intent' and 'urgency' fields, the agent decides the next action node to route to: if intent is 'billing' or urgency is 'critical', it routes to 'human_review'; if intent is 'question' or 'feature', it routes to 'search_documentation'; if intent is 'bug', it routes to 'bug_tracking'; otherwise, it routes to 'draft_response'.

You can handle exceptions during tool execution by using LangChain agent middleware that wraps the tool call and converts exceptions into ToolMessages the model can handle, preventing the agent from stopping.

An example middleware function named handle_tool_errors catches exceptions during tool calls and returns a ToolMessage with an error content prompting to check input and try again, including the exception message.
This middleware is applied when creating the agent by passing it in the middleware parameter of create_agent, allowing the agent to continue running and retry with corrected inputs.

Alternatively, you can customize error handling using the handle_errors parameter in ToolStrategy to provide a custom error message or specify exception types on which to retry, enabling retries with corrected inputs.
A super-step in LangGraph is a single 'tick' of the graph where all nodes scheduled for that step execute, potentially in parallel.
In a sequential graph, each node or step corresponds to a separate super-step, producing a checkpoint after each one.
LangGraph creates a checkpoint at each super-step boundary, which is a full state snapshot that can be used to resume execution.
Within a super-step, writes from individual node executions are persisted as tasks, enabling recovery of successful nodes' outputs if another node in the same super-step fails.
Execution can only be resumed from a checkpoint at a super-step boundary, not mid-function inside a node.
When resuming execution after an interrupt or retry, the affected node runs again from the start of its function, so node logic should be idempotent.
You can handle user input during a continuous event processing loop in LangGraph by using event streaming with human-in-the-loop (HITL) interrupts.

Use the typed projections returned by graph.stream_events(..., version="v3") in a loop until the run finishes, streaming AI responses token-by-token via stream.messages, observing per-step state snapshots via stream.values, detecting interrupts via stream.interrupted and reading their payloads from stream.interrupts.

When an interrupt is detected (stream.interrupted is true), read the interrupt payload from stream.interrupts, get user input based on the interrupt info, then resume execution by calling stream_events again with Command(resume=user_response) and repeat until stream.interrupted is false.

A typical code pattern involves initializing stream_input with the initial input, then in a while loop calling graph.stream_events(stream_input, config=config, version="v3"), streaming message chunks as they arrive, checking for interrupts after the run finishes or pauses, and if interrupted, getting user input and setting stream_input to Command(resume=user_response) to resume.
You can configure a node to retry an operation multiple times by passing a RetryPolicy to the retry_policy parameter of add_node.

RetryPolicy has parameters such as max_attempts to set the maximum number of attempts including the first, initial_interval for seconds before the first retry, backoff_factor to multiply the interval after each retry, max_interval for maximum seconds between retries, jitter to add random jitter, and retry_on to specify exceptions to retry on.
The retry policy automatically re-runs a failed node attempt based on exception type and backoff settings.
Retries are part of fault tolerance mechanisms that LangGraph provides to respond to node failures, including retries, timeouts, and error handling.
You can handle process termination signals like SIGTERM by using a RunControl object from langgraph.runtime and calling its request_drain() method to signal the program to stop gracefully.
A recommended pattern is to set a signal handler for SIGTERM that calls control.request_drain("sigterm"), allowing the program to finish ongoing tasks before exiting.

When request_drain() is called, it does not cancel running asyncio tasks or kill threads, so for a hard upper bound on shutdown time, you should pair drain with a graceful timeout and task cancellation.
If the program is stopped early due to drain, it raises a GraphDrained exception, which you can catch to handle the shutdown and optionally resume later with the same configuration.
The core agent loop involves calling a model, letting it choose tools to execute, and finishing when it calls no more tools.

A typical agent loop consists of two main steps: 1) Model call - calls the LLM with a prompt and available tools, returns either a response or a request to execute tools; 2) Tool execution - executes the tools that the LLM requested, returns tool results.
This loop continues until the LLM decides to finish.
Middleware exposes hooks before and after each of the core agent loop steps.
Middleware provides two styles of hooks to intercept agent execution: node-style hooks and wrap-style hooks.
Node-style hooks run sequentially at specific execution points such as before the agent starts, before each model call, after each model response, and after the agent completes.
Wrap-style hooks run around each call, giving control over execution, such as around each model call and around each tool call.

Middleware allows hooking into any step in the agent lifecycle to update context (modify state, update conversation history, save insights) or jump in the lifecycle (skip steps or repeat calls based on context).
The CustomerComplaint model defines three fields: issue_type, severity, and description.
The issue_type field represents the type of issue and can be one of 'product', 'service', 'shipping', or 'billing'.
The severity field represents the severity of the complaint and can be 'low', 'medium', or 'high'.
The description field is a string that provides a brief description of the complaint.

The save_preference tool updates user preferences in the store by first reading existing preferences for the user from the store using store.get with the key ('preferences',) and the user_id from the runtime context.
It then merges the new preference key and value into the existing preferences dictionary (or creates a new dictionary if none exist).
Finally, it writes the updated preferences back to the store using store.put with the key ('preferences',), the user_id, and the updated preferences dictionary.
The snapshot_frequency parameter in a DeltaChannel controls how often a full snapshot of the channel's state is written, specifically every K pregel steps if snapshot_frequency=K is set.
Setting snapshot_frequency bounds the read depth to at most K steps, which limits the read latency when reconstructing the channel state.
Higher values of snapshot_frequency reduce storage overhead but increase read latency, while lower values bound latency more tightly at the cost of larger checkpoints.
If snapshot_frequency is None (the default), snapshots are skipped entirely, which is appropriate when reads are rare or threads are short.
The llm_calls state variable tracks the number of LLM calls made during the agent's execution.
In the agent function, model_response holds the result of calling the language model (LLM) with the current messages.
The agent uses model_response to check if the model has requested any tool calls by inspecting model_response.tool_calls.
If there are tool calls, the agent executes those tools and updates the messages with the model_response and tool results, then calls the LLM again to get a new model_response.
This loop continues until the model_response indicates no more tool calls, after which the final model_response is added to messages and returned.
You import IndexConfig from langgraph.store.base and use it to configure the embedding function and embedding dimensions.
When creating a PostgresStore using from_conn_string, you pass an IndexConfig instance to the index parameter, specifying the embed function and dims.
After creating the PostgresStore with the IndexConfig, you call store.setup() before using the store.
The TypeScript quickstart guide for LangGraph can be found at https://docs.langchain.com/oss/javascript/langgraph/quickstart.md.
You should use headless tools with IndexedDB when the work depends on the environment, device, or UI that only exists on the client, such as browser APIs including IndexedDB.
Headless tools run where the user's app runs (typically the browser), not inside the server process, making them suitable for client-side operations like IndexedDB.
You create llm_with_tools by calling the bind_tools method on an existing LLM instance and passing a list of tools to it.
The tools can be user-defined functions decorated with @tool or simple functions, and they are passed as a list to bind_tools.
After binding, the resulting llm_with_tools can invoke the LLM with input that triggers tool calls, which the model requests to execute.
You initialize embeddings using langchain.embeddings by calling the function init_embeddings with a model string, for example: embeddings = init_embeddings("openai:text-embedding-3-small").
This embeddings object can then be used in a memory store or vector store for semantic search.

You specify the ask_database function as a tool with a function specification that includes its name, description, and parameters, where the parameter 'query' is a string containing the SQL query to execute.
The function ask_database is implemented to execute the SQL query against a SQLite database connection and return the results or an error message.
To use the function in a chat model, you pass the tools list including ask_database to the chat completions API call with tool_choice='auto'.

After the model generates a response indicating a function call, you extract the function name and parameters from the response, call ask_database with the SQL query, append the results to the messages list, and then call the chat completions API again with the updated messages to get the final response.
The URL of the article about cross-encoders referenced in the passage from weaviate.io is https://weaviate.io/blog/cross-encoders-as-reranker.
After calling requests.get(URL), if the response status code is 200, the code loads the JSON content from the response and extracts the 'results' field.
It initializes an empty list called places.
It iterates over the first two places in the results.
For each place, it retrieves the place_id and calls get_place_details(place_id, API_KEY) to get detailed information about the place.
From the place details, it extracts the place name, the first place type excluding 'food' and 'point_of_interest', the rating, total number of user ratings, and the vicinity (address).
The system_input_prompt variable contains a detailed instruction prompt for a helpful assistant to generate policies for a support agent at a fictional company to follow.
It instructs the assistant to create step-by-step instructions for handling customer inquiries, including decision logic for different customer categories and requirements for specific actions.
The query_graph function takes a JSON response string, parses it, and creates embeddings for each key-value pair in the JSON using the create_embedding function.
These embeddings are stored in a dictionary with keys formatted as '<key>Embedding' and values as the corresponding embeddings.
The function then generates a Cypher query string using create_query(response) and queries the graph database with this query and the embeddings as parameters.
The graph database uses these embeddings to perform a similarity search, likely using cosine similarity, to find products related to the entities extracted from the user query.
The blog post on openai.com that discusses GPT-3 applications is titled 'GPT3 Apps Blog Post' and can be found at https://openai.com/blog/gpt-3-apps/.
To create a function to find sensitive information in text, define a custom detector function that accepts a string and returns a list of PIIMatch objects with details about each detected PII.
The detector function can use regex strings, RegExp objects with flags, or custom functions for complex validation logic.
Detected PII can be handled with options such as 'block' (raise exception), 'redact' (replace with [REDACTED_{PII_TYPE}]), 'mask' (partially mask), or 'hash' (replace with deterministic hash).

LangChain provides built-in PII detection middleware that supports these handling strategies and can be configured to check user messages before model calls, AI messages after model calls, and tool result messages after execution.
To delay a node's operation until other tasks finish in a workflow with uneven path lengths, you can use the graph API's defer node execution feature.
Setting defer=True on a node postpones its execution until all pending tasks in the graph are completed, regardless of branch lengths.
For example, in a workflow where branches have different lengths, setting defer=True on node 'd' ensures it waits until the entire longer branch finishes before executing.
Alternatively, if every branch always runs, you can use a list of start nodes in add_edge to run a node once after all listed nodes complete, but this behaves differently from defer=True.

Middleware can extend the agent's state with custom properties to track state across execution and share data between hooks, enabling maintenance and sharing of state information across different stages of an agent's execution.
State is the shared memory accessible to all nodes in your agent, used to keep track of everything the agent learns and decides as it works through the process.

Agent state can be customized by defining a state schema class inheriting from AgentState and passing it as the state_schema parameter when creating the agent, allowing structured state information to be maintained and shared.
Stores provide a mechanism to persist information across threads and conversations, enabling sharing of state information beyond a single conversation and across different executions.
AI systems, specifically agents using large language models (LLMs), often fail because the LLM call inside the agent took the wrong action or didn't do what was expected.
LLMs fail for one of two reasons: either the underlying LLM is not capable enough, or the 'right' context was not passed to the LLM.
More often than not, the failure is due to the second reason: the 'right' context was not passed to the LLM, making context engineering the number one blocker for more reliable agents.
Building reliable agents is hard, and while they may work for prototypes, they often fail in real-world use cases.
LangGraph models agent workflows as graphs defined by three key components: State, Nodes, and Edges.
State is a shared data structure representing the current snapshot of the application, typically defined using a shared state schema.
Nodes are functions that encode the logic of agents, receiving the current state as input, performing computation or side-effects, and returning an updated state.
Edges are functions that determine which Node to execute next based on the current state, acting as conditional branches or fixed transitions.
By composing Nodes and Edges, complex, looping workflows that evolve the state over time can be created.
You can pause graph execution at specific points by calling the interrupt() function within your graph nodes, which suspends execution and saves the graph state using a checkpointer.
The interrupt() function accepts any JSON-serializable value that is returned to the caller when execution is paused.
Execution waits indefinitely until you resume it by invoking the graph again with a Command containing the resume value, which is passed back to the interrupt call inside the node.
Interrupts are dynamic and can be placed anywhere in your code, unlike static breakpoints which pause before or after specific nodes.
To use interrupts, you need a durable checkpointer to persist the graph state and a thread ID in your config to identify the execution state to resume from.

You can also use interrupt_before and interrupt_after parameters during graph invocation to pause execution before or after specific nodes, and then resume by invoking the graph again with None input.
LangChain provides prebuilt middleware for common use cases that are production-ready and configurable.
There is provider-agnostic middleware such as Human-in-the-loop middleware that supports workflows involving human interaction.

Shell tool middleware exposes a persistent shell session to agents for command execution, useful for system commands, automation tasks, testing, validation, file system operations, and script execution.

Shell tool middleware includes security considerations with execution policies like HostExecutionPolicy, DockerExecutionPolicy, or CodexSandboxExecutionPolicy to match deployment security requirements.
A tool call can be intercepted by defining a headless tool that does not execute locally but instead interrupts the run with a payload describing the tool call.
The app can inspect this interrupt payload, perform the action externally (e.g., in a browser, another service, or human review), and then resume the graph with the tool result.
Using the supported JS SDK hooks, headless-tool interrupts can be detected, the matching client implementation run, and the resume command submitted automatically.
The Human-in-the-Loop middleware can pause execution on tool calls for review, issuing an interrupt that halts execution and saves graph state, allowing human oversight before resuming.
Middleware ordering is important: HumanInTheLoopMiddleware should be listed before retry or error-handling middleware to avoid repeated reviews on retries.
Large language models can be guided using prompts in several ways: Instruction, Completion, Scenario, and Demonstration.
Instruction prompts tell the model explicitly what you want, often with detailed instructions at the top or bottom of the prompt.
Completion prompts start a pattern or sentence that the model completes, steering the output by how the prompt is begun.
Scenario prompts give the model a situation to play out, guiding the generation by context.
Demonstration prompts show the model what you want by including examples, either a few in the prompt or many in a fine-tuning dataset.
We can predict a numerical rating from the text of a review by using regression on the embedding of the review's text, where the score is a number between 1 and 5.
The dataset used for this task can be a subset of Amazon fine-food reviews, combining review summary and review text into a single combined text to generate embeddings.
The embeddings of the combined text are used as input features for a regression model, such as a RandomForestRegressor, to predict the review score.
The regression model is trained on a training set and evaluated on a test set, with performance metrics like mean squared error (MSE) and mean absolute error (MAE) used to assess prediction accuracy.
Using embeddings, the average error in score prediction can be about 0.53, meaning roughly half of the reviews are predicted perfectly and half are off by one star.
You can improve the relevance of academic paper results by creating a tailored cross-encoder that uses domain-specific nuances to pick the most relevant corpus for your users.
Pre-filtering the search results to limit the amount of data the cross-encoder processes is important for efficiency and effectiveness.

A typical approach is to first return a list of the top 100 or 1000 most relevant results using a classic rules-based or semantic search, then rerank this shortened list using the cross-encoder to reorder results based on detailed context or specific user needs.
Building a prompt with few-shot examples tailored to your domain and using logit bias to classify relevance as yes/no helps tune the cross-encoder for better reranking.

You can retrieve a list of local venues based on user preferences by integrating the Google Places API with custom user profiles that capture individual preferences such as types of places, budget, and ratings.
The process involves fetching a user profile with preferences and location, then calling the Google Places API to find nearby places matching the place type and optional food preferences.

The function call_google_places_api fetches the customer profile, constructs a Google Places API request URL based on the user's location and preferences, sends the request, and processes the top results to return detailed place information.
Function calling can be used to activate the API call based on user input, such as 'I'm hungry', which triggers a search for relevant venues like restaurants or cafes.
The returned results include place name, type, rating, total ratings, and vicinity, providing a human-readable list of recommended venues tailored to the user's preferences and location.

GPT-4o mini can analyze images of clothing items and extract key features such as color, style, and type through an API call that returns a structured JSON with item descriptions, category, and gender.

Using the extracted features, a custom matching algorithm combined with Retrieval-Augmented Generation (RAG) searches a knowledge base for items that complement the original outfit, considering factors like color compatibility and style coherence.

Guardrails and self-correction mechanisms are implemented by sending the original image and suggested items back to GPT-4o mini to evaluate if each suggested item is a good fit, allowing the model to refine and improve its recommendations.

This approach enables practical applications such as personalized shopping assistants, virtual wardrobe applications, and fashion design and styling tools by providing accurate and contextually relevant outfit recommendations based on image analysis.
You can generate a list of API endpoint details including their identifiers, descriptions, and input parameter schemas by parsing an OpenAPI JSON schema file.
First, load the OpenAPI specification JSON file using jsonref to resolve JSON references.

Then, iterate over the paths and methods in the OpenAPI spec to extract each endpoint's operationId as the function name, description or summary as the description, and construct a parameters schema from the requestBody and parameters fields.
The parameters schema is constructed as a JSON schema object with properties for requestBody and parameters, where parameters include the input parameters with their types and required status.
This process can be implemented in a function like openapi_to_functions which returns a list of function dictionaries each containing name, description, and parameters schema.

A model can decide when to stop or continue a selection-inference cycle by using a 'halter' model that, after each inference step, assesses whether the inferences so far are sufficient to answer the question and either halts or continues the process accordingly.
The halter model prevents the generation of hallucinated guesses by allowing the process to produce no answer if it never halts, which is often preferable to incorrect answers.

To reduce generating incorrect facts (hallucinations), the model can be fine-tuned to reason about sentence labels (e.g., sen1) rather than writing out the sentences themselves, which constrains what the model can say and reduces hallucination of fake facts.
A value function can be added to assess the quality of reasoning steps and search over multiple reasoning trajectories, helping to pick the best reasoning path and improve reliability.
You can access the same memories across different threads by using the same user_id as the namespace for memories.
When invoking the graph on a new thread, specify the thread_id in the config and use the same user_id in the context to access the same memories.
Memories are stored in a store with a namespace tuple that includes the user_id, for example (user_id, "memories"), allowing access across threads.
You compile the graph with both a checkpointer (to save state to threads) and a store (to store arbitrary information accessible across threads).
In production, you can use the store's search or asearch methods with the namespace including the user_id to retrieve memories across threads.
To efficiently store versioned checkpoint data, use two SQL tables: 'checkpoints' and 'writes'.

The 'checkpoints' table should have columns: thread_id, checkpoint_ns, checkpoint_id (ULID, lexicographically sortable newest-last), parent_checkpoint_id, type, checkpoint (BYTEA), metadata (JSONB), with a primary key on (thread_id, checkpoint_ns, checkpoint_id).

The 'writes' table should have columns: thread_id, checkpoint_ns, checkpoint_id, task_id, task_path, idx, channel, type, value (BYTEA), with a primary key on (thread_id, checkpoint_ns, checkpoint_id, task_id, task_path, idx).
Because checkpoint_id is a ULID, it sorts lexicographically with larger values being newer, enabling efficient queries like 'ORDER BY checkpoint_id DESC LIMIT 1' to get the latest checkpoint.
To retrieve checkpoints ordered by newest first, query the 'checkpoints' table filtering by thread_id and checkpoint_ns, ordering by checkpoint_id descending.
Direct lookup by (thread_id, checkpoint_ns, checkpoint_id) must be O(1) or close to it, so the primary key includes these fields to avoid scanning all rows.
You can log the execution and results of a tool call in an agent's processing pipeline by implementing custom middleware that wraps the tool call and logs details before and after execution.
The custom middleware can print the tool name, arguments, and whether the tool completed successfully or failed with an exception.
This middleware approach integrates with the agent's tool call handling by wrapping the tool call request and its handler.
A checkpoint's metadata includes information such as the step number, node, triggers, path, checkpoint namespace, source, writes, parents, and thread ID.
A checkpoint's configuration details include configurable parameters like thread ID, checkpoint namespace, and checkpoint ID.
Changing the sequence of user prompts or reordering interrupt calls can cause the wrong cached resume value to be matched with an interrupt, leading to incorrect results.
LangGraph matches cached results and resume values to calls by their position in the replay, so shifting that position can cause the wrong cached value to be replayed against a different call.
Looping over a list that may change during execution is risky because the number of interrupts can change between executions, causing index mismatches.
Interrupt calls must not be reordered or conditionally skipped within a node, as this changes the order and causes index mismatches on resume.
You can enable an agent to run system commands securely within a persistent shell session by using the ShellToolMiddleware middleware.
ShellToolMiddleware exposes a persistent shell session to agents for command execution, useful for system commands, automation, testing, and file operations.

To configure security, use appropriate execution policies such as HostExecutionPolicy (full host access), DockerExecutionPolicy (isolated Docker container), or CodexSandboxExecutionPolicy (sandboxed execution) depending on your security requirements.
You can specify the workspace root directory, optional startup commands, and redaction rules to sanitize command output.
An example to create an agent with ShellToolMiddleware using HostExecutionPolicy is provided, showing how to set workspace_root and execution_policy.
You can specify a fallback function for errors in all nodes of a StateGraph by using the set_node_defaults method with the error_handler parameter.
This fallback error handler applies to every node in the graph unless a specific node overrides it by passing its own error_handler parameter in add_node.
Per-node error handlers take precedence over the graph-wide default error handler set by set_node_defaults.
An example shows setting a graph-wide error_handler mark_process_failed via set_node_defaults, and overriding it for a specific node charge_payment with refund_payment as its error_handler.
The execution environment and security policies for the shell session are controlled by the execution policy option in ShellToolMiddleware.
There are three execution policies available: HostExecutionPolicy, DockerExecutionPolicy, and CodexSandboxExecutionPolicy.
HostExecutionPolicy provides full host access and is the default, suitable for trusted environments.
DockerExecutionPolicy launches a separate Docker container for each agent run, providing stronger isolation.
CodexSandboxExecutionPolicy reuses the Codex CLI sandbox for additional syscall and filesystem restrictions.

You can retrieve the current status of a paused thread by calling graph.get_state(config), which returns the latest checkpoint including the node where the thread is paused and any pending interrupts.

You can retrieve the full history of a paused thread by calling graph.get_state_history(config), which returns a chronological list of StateSnapshot objects for the thread, with the most recent checkpoint first.

To view detailed thread state including messages and metadata, you can use checkpointer.get_tuple(config) with the thread_id, optionally specifying a checkpoint_id to get a specific checkpoint or the latest checkpoint by default.
You can enhance an agent with tool approval by adding human-in-the-loop patterns that allow tool approval before execution and batch approval.
Subgraphs can be created for complex multi-step operations to enhance agent capabilities.
Streaming can be added to show real-time progress to users, managed via the Functional API's entrypoint decorator which handles streaming and execution flow.
Observability can be added with LangSmith for debugging and monitoring complex agent behavior, including tracing execution paths and capturing runtime metrics.
Tool integration can be enhanced by integrating more tools such as web search, database queries, API calls, and server-side tools provided by chat model providers.
Retry logic can be implemented using prebuilt middleware like Tool retry, which automatically retries failed tool calls with exponential backoff.

When delta channels are absent from checkpoint data, LangGraph calls saver.get_delta_channel_history to retrieve all writes to that channel in the ancestor chain up to the nearest snapshot, and optionally a stored DeltaSnapshot blob at the nearest ancestor that has one.
The runtime reconstructs the live value by calling channel.from_checkpoint with the seed snapshot and then channel.replay_writes with the retrieved writes.

Encryption is automatically enabled when using LangSmith if the environment variable LANGGRAPH_AES_KEY is present.
You can restrict the number of times an agent calls a specific tool or all tools by using the ToolCallLimitMiddleware.
ToolCallLimitMiddleware can be configured with parameters such as tool_name to specify a particular tool or left unspecified to apply limits globally across all tools.
You can set thread_limit and run_limit parameters to control the maximum number of tool calls across threads and per run respectively.

Exit behaviors when limits are reached include 'continue' (default, blocks exceeded calls with error messages but agent continues), 'error' (raises exception immediately), and 'end' (stops with ToolMessage + AI message, for single-tool scenarios).

Example usage includes creating an agent with middleware like ToolCallLimitMiddleware(thread_limit=20, run_limit=10) for global limits and ToolCallLimitMiddleware(tool_name='search', thread_limit=5, run_limit=3) for tool-specific limits.
You can limit the execution time of an asynchronous node in LangGraph by using the timeout parameter with add_node to specify how long a single async node invocation can run.
The timeout parameter accepts a number (seconds), a datetime.timedelta, or a TimeoutPolicy for separate run and idle limits.
Node timeouts only apply to async nodes; setting timeout on a sync node causes a compile-time error.
If you want to wrap blocking I/O with a timeout, use asyncio.to_thread inside an async node.

Section titles come with descriptions that give a brief overview of the main topics and concepts covered in that section, aiding quick understanding.
Using section titles and descriptions allows for generating a plan for a report, which can be used to write and synthesize sections separately, making the content easier to navigate and skim.
